subject_area: Operating systems — core concepts and mechanisms
course_intent: Teach the foundational concepts and mechanisms of operating systems — students should leave able to explain how an OS manages processes, memory, files, and concurrency, and reason about classical algorithms (scheduling, page replacement, deadlock handling, synchronization) using the Silberschatz textbook framing.
depth_bound: Recommendations stay at the level of classical OS concepts and algorithm-level reasoning aligned with the Silberschatz textbook. Kernel-internals deep dives, hands-on systems programming projects (e.g., writing a scheduler in C), distributed OS theory, and modern container/virtualization internals are beyond this course's depth.
key_topics: OS structure, kernel/user mode, and system calls
Deadlock characterization, prevention, avoidance, and detection
Contiguous memory allocation, segmentation, and paging
Virtual memory, demand paging, and page replacement (FIFO, OPT, LRU)
File system interface, access methods, and FCB structures
File allocation methods (contiguous, linked, indexed, FAT)
one_liner: Classical undergraduate operating systems course covering processes, synchronization, deadlocks, memory management, virtual memory, and file systems at a conceptual + algorithmic level — does NOT include hands-on kernel implementation, modern OS topics like containers/virtualization internals, or distributed systems.
